arxiv-2610-39302.text:
Gist: Despite the request framing, this is not a robotics paper. It is a representation-learning paper. It turns the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) into a theorem for Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs). Encoders trained separately on different modalities learn the same embedding up to one rotation when their positive pairs are two observations of the same scene ("good views"). The paper also argues that next-token prediction is a "bad-view" JEPA, and shows empirically that a 109M-parameter text JEPA aligns with vision models better than language models up to 72B parameters.

Question: The PRH, the claim that vision and language models converge to a shared representation as they scale, has so far been an empirical observation without a proof. The paper asks when models trained separately on different modalities provably learn the same representation. It also asks whether that answer gives a training recipe, rather than relying on scale alone.

Method: The world is modeled as a finite set of states, each modality renders it injectively, and the JEPA loss is a prediction term plus a rotation-invariant anti-collapse term. The predictor is the identity; the paper explicitly does not cover learned or action-conditioned predictors. The main results are:
- Renderings only change coordinates, so if all modalities share one positive-pair distribution and the minimizers are unique up to rotation, every encoder recovers the same world embedding up to a rotation (Theorem 1).
- With MSE plus whitening, the minimizer is the spectral embedding of the positive-pair graph, unique under an eigengap (Proposition 1).
- If positives differ across modalities, a Davis–Kahan-style bound limits misalignment by the kernel mismatch divided by the eigengap (Theorem 2). On 300 synthetic worlds the measured error stays at or below 18% of the bound.
- With per-observation nuisance (wording, viewpoint), any embedding direction spent on nuisance is lost for alignment (Theorem 3). Corruptions of a single observation spend directions on nuisance whenever they preserve it more than the world's k-th direction (Proposition 3).
- Views and data together determine an induced world kernel (Theorem 4).
- Next-token prediction is cast as a JEPA whose positives are a prefix and its continuation and whose anti-collapse term is the softmax log-partition, identified only up to an invertible linear map (Proposition 4).

In practice, good-view training uses LeJEPA/SIGReg (λ=0.02). Text views are drawn from different captions of the same image, each trimmed to a random span with 15% masking.

Robots and setup: There are no robots, robot sensors, simulators or control tasks. The data are:
- Flickr30k: 29k images with 5 captions each.
- MSR-VTT video: 7k training clips with 20 captions each, the only setting where the image side gets good views (different frames).
- COCO.
- Recap-DataComp: each image's alt-text plus two LLaVA (LLaMA-3-8B) recaptions, scaled up to the texts of 940M images.
- The PRH paper's WIT-1024 benchmark.

The models are a ViT-S/16 image JEPA and BERT text encoders of 11M–335M parameters trained from scratch, scored against frozen DINOv2/DINOv3, CLIP, MAE and I-JEPA. Baselines are Qwen2.5 (0.5–72B), Llama-3 8B/70B, Mistral-7B, Qwen3-8B, CLIP's text encoder and all-mpnet-base-v2. Metrics are mutual 10-NN, unbiased linear CKA, and retrieval R@1 through a single orthogonal map fitted on pairs.

Results:
- Flickr, separately trained image JEPA: the good-view text JEPA reaches mutual 10-NN .062 versus .047 (bad views) and .042 (next-token), and R@1 .044 versus .027 and .021.
- Flickr, frozen DINOv2: R@1 is .246 versus .133 and .118.
- Nuisance measurement: the scene explains a fraction .804 of the good-view embedding, against .655 and .608, matching the theory's predicted ordering.
- Scale on WIT-1024: the 109M good-view JEPA trained on the texts of 940M images reaches .184 with DINOv2 ViT-B. This beats Qwen2.5-72B (.154), Llama-3-70B (.151) and CLIP's text encoder (.124). Its CKA is .507 versus .418, and with CLIP ViT-H it scores .230 versus .210.
- Sample efficiency: on the same corpus, good views reach next-token's 900M-sample alignment with 21.6M samples (.109 vs .111), 42 times fewer.
- Scaling law: an alignment law in the good-view fraction and samples seen predicted 85 unseen runs with RMSE .0093, versus .0096 seed-to-seed. It overestimates good-view runs at 320M samples.
- Captioning: a captioner whose only part fitted on pairs is one orthonormal map (30k Flickr pairs) reaches COCO CIDEr .838 and MSR-VTT video CIDEr .246.
- Pair-free alignment (Schnaus et al. protocol): ImageNet-100 top-5 is 64.4% versus 47.6% for Qwen3-8B rerun and 56% for the best they reported. CLIP's text encoder still gets 68.7%.

Ablations: Trimming captions into spans is the knob that matters. Using whole captions as views drops R@1 from .246 to .185. Masking, number of views, batch size, width and schedule move the mean by at most .016. Without gradient clipping, some runs collapse abruptly. On MSR-VTT, good views on both sides give mutual 10-NN .067, against .039 when neither side has them, with the text side contributing most.

Limitations: The theory assumes a finite world, injective renderings, population optima and an identity predictor. Uniqueness up to rotation is not proven for SIGReg, and no experiment meets Theorem 1's hypotheses exactly. Good views require knowing which texts describe the same scene. On Recap, two of three texts come from a CLIP-based captioner; without it, good views reach only .060 on WIT versus .107. At the 940M scale, the SIGReg weight was chosen after seeing WIT results, and a seed at the other weight scored .121. There is minor benchmark overlap with the training data. The image side is mostly bad-view crops, and hyperparameters were tuned only for the good-view JEPA.

Takeaway for a robotics researcher: Read it only if you care about JEPA theory or about aligning separately trained sensor or modality encoders. The transferable lesson is to define positives as multiple observations of the same state, such as different cameras or frames, rather than augmentations of one observation. The paper's world-model analysis is limited: it excludes action-conditioned predictors and notes that camera viewpoint, a nuisance for cross-modal alignment, is something an acting agent must track. Section 2 (theory) and Sections 3.2–3.3 (view ablations, video) are the most relevant; the LLM-scaling and captioning sections can be skimmed.

arxiv-2611-04492.text:
Gist: The paper presents "3D World Simulator," an action-conditioned world model that predicts the future of a manipulation scene in a shared 3D latent space instead of in image space. A hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder compresses RGB-D point clouds, with optional tactile points, into a compact voxel latent. A latent dynamics model rolls that latent forward given robot actions, and the decoded output is a set of 3D Gaussian particles plus tactile particles. Because the output is explicitly 3D, the model can render consistent RGB-D from arbitrary viewpoints, including moving wrist cameras, and its tactile predictions stay geometrically aligned with contact surfaces. The authors use it for synthetic policy-training data, policy evaluation, and zero-shot MPC on unseen objects, and claim interactive rollout at 50 Hz.

Question: Most action-conditioned world models, such as Cosmos, IWS and video diffusion models, operate in 2D pixel space. This makes multi-view consistency and long-horizon spatial coherence hard to maintain, and it makes contact-geometry relationships hard to represent. Existing 3D dynamics models like PGND, PointWorld and ParticleFormer have their own limits: they rely on point-tracking supervision or object-specific state representations, and they usually do not target photorealistic rendering for visuomotor policies. The paper asks whether a correspondence-free, scene-level 3D latent can provide geometry, appearance and touch in one interface while staying stable over long open-loop horizons.

Method: The autoencoder works in three steps.
- The point cloud has 7 channels per point (xyz, RGB, tactile). It is voxelized and averaged per occupied cell.
- Strided sparse 3D convolutions downsample it to a unit-normalized 8-channel latent grid: 32×16×32 for ALOHA and 32³ for Deform360.
- A coarse-to-fine decoder upsamples with transposed convolutions, predicting occupancy at three resolutions. A lightweight MLP then turns each occupied voxel into continuous particles over two refinement stages. Each particle carries Gaussian parameters (color via degree-1 spherical harmonics, anisotropic scale, rotation, opacity).

The autoencoder is trained with four losses: per-level occupancy BCE, local bidirectional Chamfer plus color L1, rendered RGB-D loss (L1/SSIM/LPIPS plus depth L1), and a consistency loss between latents of two independent subsamples of the same cloud.

The dynamics model is a 3D U-Net. It takes 5 history latents and encodes each frame with shared 3D convolutions. At an 8×4×8 coarse grid it alternates spatial attention with causal temporal attention, and it injects action, timestamp and noise-level embeddings via an MLP. It directly regresses the next latent in one forward pass. For stability, training uses three measures: K-step autoregressive rollouts with a discounted L2 loss (γ=0.95), a curriculum on K, and history-latent noise with standard deviation up to 0.4.

Each model trains in about 16 hours on a single RTX 5090. Wrist-camera rendering requires a separately fine-tuned decoder head. Separating robot, object and table, which is needed to compose the output with other Gaussian backgrounds or new kinematic robot models, also requires fine-tuning.

Robots and setup: The main platform is an ALOHA bimanual robot with FlexiTac tactile sensors on each fingertip. Sensing comes from three static RealSense D455 stereo cameras (one top-down and two forward-facing) and two wrist-mounted RealSense D405s. Depth is computed with FoundationStereo, and tactile pad positions come from forward kinematics.

There are six tasks, each with about 200 teleoperated episodes (about 2 hours): Part Assembly, Cloth Folding, T Pushing, Box Packing, Rope Threading and Marker Insertion. Together they cover rigid, articulated and deformable objects.

For scaling, the model is trained on Deform360. That dataset contains 198 objects, 1,980 sequences, more than 215 hours of footage from 41 cameras, and bimanual tactile grippers. Training on it uses object points only, because the dataset provides only object-centric depth.

Baselines:
- 2D video models: Cosmos, Robot4DGen and IWS, adapted for multi-view and depth.
- 3D particle models: PGND, PointWorld and ParticleFormer, supervised with CoTracker tracks.

Downstream policies are ACT, Diffusion Policy, π0.5 (LoRA) and Cosmos Policy. Planning uses MPPI borrowed from PGND on an unseen single-arm ALOHA setup.

Results: On ALOHA, metrics are averaged over 6 tasks and 200-step open-loop rollouts. The proposed model leads on every metric:

| Metric | Ours | Best baseline |
|---|---|---|
| PSNR | 23.24 | 20.59 (Robot4DGen) |
| LPIPS | 0.240 | 0.340 (Robot4DGen) |
| Depth Abs Rel | 0.097 | 0.147 (Cosmos) |
| δ<1.25 | 0.913 | 0.833 (Cosmos) |
| Scene Chamfer | 7.72 | 10.43 (Robot4DGen) |
| Object Chamfer | 11.52 | 15.97 (Robot4DGen) |
| Tactile L1 | 0.081 | 0.128 (Robot4DGen) |

The 3D particle baselines do worse on geometry than the video models (Chamfer 13.78–17.11).

On Deform360, with 150-step rollouts, the picture is mixed:
- Training objects: the model beats ParticleFormer on PSNR (18.6 vs 18.0), LPIPS (0.26 vs 0.30) and Chamfer (9.6 vs 10.5 mm).
- Held-out objects: it keeps the geometry lead (12.1 vs 13.4 mm) but loses on appearance (PSNR 14.8 vs 15.6, LPIPS 0.43 vs 0.31). The authors attribute this to the baselines moving pre-fitted Gaussian splats, whereas this model generates appearance from scratch.

Policy training and evaluation: Each task uses 100 demos, and success rates are averaged over the four policy architectures. Values below are read approximately from a bar chart, since exact numbers are not tabulated:

| Task | Real-data policies | Simulator-data policies |
|---|---|---|
| Part Assembly, visuo-tactile | ~0.8 | ~0.68 |
| Part Assembly, vision-only (real) | ~0.17 | — |
| Cloth Folding, front plus wrist views | ~0.95 | ~1.0 |
| T Pushing, novel viewpoint | ~0.8 | ~0.68 |

For policy evaluation, checkpoints were each evaluated 20 times in the simulator and 20 times in the real world. Simulator and real success rates correlate at r = 0.958 (Part Assembly), 0.965 (Cloth Folding) and 0.859 (T Pushing).

Zero-shot MPC with the Deform360-trained model on four unseen objects reaches final Chamfer distances of 0.031 (cloth), 0.024 (rope), 0.035 (foam) and 0.047 (sloth). These results are presented without baseline comparisons.

Limitations and caveats: The paper reports no ablations. It does not isolate the contributions of the particle stage, the consistency loss, history noise, the K-step curriculum or the tactile channel, beyond the tactile-versus-no-tactile policy comparison. The 50 Hz claim is not broken down by component.

The model is bounded to a fixed cropped workspace. Composition with backgrounds and new robots, as well as wrist views, depends on extra fine-tuning. Appearance generalization to unseen objects lags behind splat-based baselines.

Policy experiments rest on small samples (20 trials, wide Clopper-Pearson intervals), and the success rates are shown only graphically. It is not fully clear how the simulator demonstrations were produced. The particle baselines were trained on CoTracker pseudo-tracks, which may handicap them relative to their original setups.

Takeaways: The paper is worth reading if you work on world models for policy evaluation or data generation, especially with wrist cameras, novel viewpoints or tactile sensing. Its main idea is a correspondence-free voxel latent decoded to Gaussians, which gives multi-view consistency and spatially grounded touch at interactive rates. That idea is simple, and the comparison against both 2D video and 3D particle families is fairly broad. Read it with skepticism about the lack of ablations and the small-sample policy results. Readers mainly interested in open-world generalization should note the weaker held-out appearance results.

arxiv-2203-01153.text:
Gist: InsertionNet 2.0 is a supervised residual policy for peg-in-hole style insertion. It regresses pose corrections from stereo wrist images plus force/torque direction, and it learns from about 150 self-collected samples per plug, with no RL, demonstrations or reward engineering. It extends the authors' earlier InsertionNet in four ways: two wrist cameras, data collected along free-space trajectories so the robot no longer has to touch the socket surface first, an auxiliary contrastive loss, and a relation-network head that enables one-shot transfer and simple multi-step tasks. It reports near-perfect success on 16 real connectors and threads.

Question: Online RL and Sim2Real approaches to contact-rich insertion are expensive, risky for hardware, and limited by simulation fidelity. The original InsertionNet avoided these problems with backward-learned regression, but it used a single wrist camera. That camera could not resolve depth ambiguity, so the robot had to touch the socket before correcting. The paper asks three things: whether a multiview, multimodal regression approach can remove that contact requirement, whether it can cut sample needs using unlabeled data, and whether it can generalize to unseen plugs and multi-step sequences.

Method: Data collection uses "general backward learning." A human first inserts the plug and the final pose L_final is registered. The robot then repeatedly moves under impedance control to random targets drawn from a normal distribution around L_final (r0 = 10 mm, θ0 = 10°). These alternate between a "high" target, up to 50 mm above the hole, and a "low" target at hole height. Along each trajectory it logs stereo images, force and moment, labeled with L_final minus the current pose. The authors report that uniform sampling put too many points far from the hole.

Method (network and policy): A single ResNet18 encoder is trained jointly on three losses.
- An InfoNCE contrastive loss with a Polyak-averaged momentum encoder (m = 0.999), in the style of CURL, applied to the stacked 6-channel stereo image.
- A "Delta" regression loss predicting the 6-DoF correction from images and force.
- A "Relation" loss that takes two images of the same task and predicts the difference in their corrections.

Force and moment are fed in as unit direction vectors only. The images get heavy augmentation, including random convolution, erasing and color jitter, applied consistently within each batch. At runtime, a coarse main policy from InsertionNet 1 brings the gripper near the hole. Within a radius R, the residual policy outputs (Δx, Δy, Δθx, Δθy, Δθz) while z is lowered at a fixed rate. The Delta head is used for standard tasks. The Relation head is conditioned on a stored goal image and is used for one-shot and multi-step tasks.

Robots and setup: The robot is a UR5e arm with two Intel RealSense D435 wrist cameras, each tilted 45° and aimed between the fingers. Force/torque comes from the UR5e's built-in estimate, sampled at 500 Hz over RTDE, with commands sent at 125 Hz. There is no simulator; everything is on the real robot. The 16 tasks reuse the InsertionNet 1 set: AC 2-pin and 3-pin, AUX, DC12V, RJ45, HDMI, keys, power cord, USB, USB-C, VGA, and circle, half-circle, triangle, cube, cylinder and rectangle "pulley"/thread pieces. Each plug gets 150 collected samples, which are expanded via augmentation and pairing to about 192k training samples. Training takes 5–15 minutes on two RTX 2080 Ti GPUs.

Evaluation: For each task, test start poses are sampled uniformly in a box around the hole, and 200 consecutive trials are run with the peg not fixed in the gripper, so misalignment accumulates. Success means reaching z − z0 < 1 mm within 10 s.

Results: The Delta policy's worst success rate is 97.5%, on the cylindrical thread, and most tasks score 100%. The largest gains over InsertionNet 1.0 are:
- VGA: 78.5% to 100%
- HDMI: 90.5% to 99.5%
- USB-C: 91.5% to 100%
- Keys: 90.5% to 100%
- Power cord: 94% to 98%

A few tasks dropped slightly, for example triangular thread from 100% to 99.5% and cylindrical thread from 100% to 97.5%. Reported mean times are 0–1.54 s, versus 1.3–5 s for v1. However, v2 times subtract the mean reaching time, so the time comparison is not apples-to-apples. The v1 baseline also ran on a Franka Panda, and the authors themselves credit part of the gain to the UR5e's controller.

Ablations and sample efficiency: On AC 2-pin (50 trials per point), success reaches 100% at about 40 samples, and completion time approaches its minimum at about 150 samples. With 20 labeled plus 150 unlabeled samples, the contrastive term raised Relation-policy success from 20% to 100% and Delta-policy success from 70% to 100%. In a separate ablation on AC 2-pin, USB and yellow thread, contrastive loss made no noticeable difference for the Delta policy but gave the Relation policy roughly 20% higher success and lower time variance, mostly with small datasets.

Robustness: The Delta policy was trained on 300 samples with grasp angles of 0° and ±15°. It went 50/50 under grasp errors up to 45°, room lights switched on and off, random obstacles, and the board being moved during execution. The Relation policy failed with obstacles unless extra data was collected, and it needed more data to handle large grasp changes.

Transfer and multi-step: A model trained on 15 plugs was tested on the held-out red half-circle thread. Given only a goal image, the Relation policy went 50/50, while the Delta policy went 0/50. The Delta policy recovers with about 20 new samples, versus 150 from scratch. The multi-step task was inserting a key, turning the lock, and turning it back, using a pre-stored stereo goal image for each step and similarity-based step switching. It scored 50/50, even though the training data never visited the inserted or turned states.

Limitations: There is no comparison against RL, LfD or other contemporary insertion methods, only against the authors' own prior system on a different robot. The "minimal contact" claim is not quantified with contact-force statistics. Policies are trained per plug and require a human-registered final pose. The test-region bounds B_xy, B_θ and B_z are not specified. Robustness, transfer and multi-step results rest on 50 trials each, with a single held-out object described as "somewhat similar" to the training set. Several reported effects, such as the stability gains and the robustness comparisons, are only qualitative.

Takeaway: Read it if you want a practical, low-data, fast-to-train recipe for real-world tight-tolerance insertion. Useful details include the stereo wrist-camera placement, trajectory-wide backward data collection, direction-only force inputs, and a relation head for goal-image-conditioned transfer. Skim it if you need rigorous baselines or analysis of generalization limits.

arxiv-2606-24457.text:
Gist: The paper presents Lite Any Stereo V2 (LAS2), a family of lightweight stereo disparity networks (S, M, L feed-forward and H iterative) meant to generalize zero-shot to unseen real scenes while running fast on GPUs and embedded hardware. It is relevant to robotics because it targets dense metric depth from a stereo pair on a Jetson-class device without per-domain fine-tuning. The authors report state-of-the-art accuracy among efficient stereo methods along with clearly lower measured latency.

Question: The paper challenges the common assumption that small, fast stereo networks cannot match the zero-shot generalization of large, foundation-prior models such as FoundationStereo or MonSter++. Those large models run out of memory on edge devices. The paper also addresses two further gaps. First, prior efficient designs were optimized for theoretical MACs rather than real latency. Second, recent "real-time" iterative methods such as Fast-FoundationStereo and RT-MonSter++ are only fast on high-end GPUs.

Method: The architecture uses a FasterNet ImageNet-pretrained encoder producing multi-scale features, which are fused at 1/4 resolution.
- A correlation cost volume is built with a maximum disparity of 192.
- Cost aggregation is a 2D-only U-Net built from FasterNet-style blocks, replacing the hybrid 3D-2D aggregation of the earlier LAS. Variants scale the aggregation depth (1/2/4, 4/8/16 and 8/16/32 layers per level for S, M and L).
- Disparity comes from soft-argmax followed by convex upsampling.
- LAS2-H reuses LAS2-M as the initializer and adds a group-wise correlation volume and an all-pairs volume, refined over 4 selective-ConvGRU iterations.

Training happens in three stages:
- Stage 1 is supervised training on about 1.8M synthetic pairs (SceneFlow, FallingThings, FSD, CREStereo, VKITTI2, TartanAir, Dynamic Replica).
- Stage 2 is self-distillation: a frozen teacher sees clean inputs while the student sees strongly perturbed ones (color jitter, blur, gamma), with a cosine feature-alignment loss.
- Stage 3 trains on about 0.5M unlabeled real pairs with dense pseudo-labels from FoundationStereo. The labels are filtered by a left-right consistency mask, an edge mask (disparity edges without image edges) and a SAM 3 sky mask. The loss is clamped per pixel at 10 so that a few high-error pixels cannot dominate early adaptation.

Robots and setup: No robot platform or robotic task is used; this is a pure perception paper.
- Hardware: latency is measured in PyTorch with torch.compile disabled at 384×1248 on RTX 4090, A5000, A100 and H200 GPUs, and on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX 8G at 10W, 20W and MAXN power modes.
- Real-world training data: Flickr1024, InStereo2k, Holopix50K, DrivingStereo, SouthKenSV and UASOL.
- Zero-shot evaluation: KITTI 2012/2015, ETH3D, Middlebury (half resolution) and the DrivingStereo weather split.
- Baselines: efficient feed-forward baselines were retrained on the same synthetic data.

Results: LAS2-M versus the prior LAS on zero-shot benchmarks (lower is better):

| Benchmark | LAS2-M | LAS |
|---|---|---|
| KITTI 2012 D1 | 2.88 | 3.04 |
| KITTI 2015 D1 | 3.61 | 3.87 |
| ETH3D Bad1 | 2.59 | 3.53 |
| Middlebury Bad2 | 5.47 | 7.51 |
| Latency, H200 / Orin MAXN | 8.1 / 101 ms | 12.7 / 193 ms |

LAS2-S runs at 6.6 ms on H200 and 81 ms on Orin. LAS2-L is the most accurate feed-forward model (KITTI 2015 D1 3.38, ETH3D 1.83).

LAS2-H versus Fast-FoundationStereo: KITTI 2012 D1 is 2.64 vs 2.90, KITTI 2015 D1 3.31 vs 3.66, ETH3D ties at 1.83, and Middlebury Bad2 is 3.71 vs 3.73. LAS2-H runs at 15.1 vs 27.3 ms on H200 and 344 vs 918 ms on Orin.

FoundationStereo remains far more accurate on ETH3D (0.49) and Middlebury (1.12), but needs 292 ms on H200 and runs out of memory on Orin.

On DrivingStereo weather, overall D1 is 7.23 for LAS2-S, 8.74 for LAS and 7.44 for LAS2-H. LAS2-H beats Fast-FoundationStereo (9.15) and even its teacher FoundationStereo (10.71), though MonSter++ is better at 5.21. On the KITTI 2015 test leaderboard, LAS2-M (fine-tuned on KITTI raw pseudo-labels) reaches D1-all 1.61, best among efficient methods; on KITTI 2012 it trails RT-MonSter++ and LAS.

Ablations: Architecture choices were selected by measured Orin latency, not MACs. FasterNet aggregation took 107 ms versus 162 ms for ConvNeXt, even though ConvNeXt had fewer MACs.

For training, the stage progression on LAS2-M moved KITTI 2012 D1 from 4.21 to 3.59 to 2.88 and Middlebury Bad2 from 7.95 to 6.91 to 5.47.
- Removing error clamping hurt every benchmark (e.g., ETH3D 3.22 vs 2.59).
- The LR mask gave the largest filtering gain, while the sky mask's effect was mixed.
- A fixed teacher beat EMA and hard-copy teachers in Stage 2.
- Adding Stereo4D or Xperience data, or using multiple teachers, did not help.
- The same recipe substantially improved LightStereo-M and BANet-2D (e.g., Middlebury Bad2 for LightStereo-M fell from 10.29 to 7.08), suggesting it is a reusable training recipe.

Limitations and takeaways: A clear accuracy gap remains to foundation-prior models, especially on ETH3D and Middlebury. The authors attribute this partly to the limited scale of high-quality real stereo data. The model still fails on reflective or transparent surfaces and under severe illumination changes. For roboticists, note three things:
- Orin latencies are measured in plain PyTorch without TensorRT or compile. Real-time rates on Orin (about 10 Hz for M at 384×1248) may improve with deployment tooling, but this is untested.
- There is no downstream robotic evaluation such as navigation or grasping.
- The strongest gains come from the pseudo-label distillation recipe, which is cheap to adopt for other lightweight stereo networks.

The paper is worth reading if you need an off-the-shelf stereo depth model on Jetson-class hardware or want a practical recipe for distilling a large stereo teacher into a small model.

arxiv-2511-08544.text:
Gist: This is not a robotics paper. It is a self-supervised visual representation learning paper from Balestriero and LeCun (Brown/NYU/Meta-FAIR). It proposes LeJEPA, a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) objective built on one claim: embeddings should follow an isotropic Gaussian distribution. A new regularizer, SIGReg, enforces that distribution and replaces the usual anti-collapse heuristics (stop-gradient, teacher–student EMA, predictors, whitening, register tokens). For a robotics researcher, the relevance is indirect. It offers a simple, stable, single-hyperparameter recipe for pretraining encoders, possibly on your own in-domain data, which could serve as a backbone for JEPA-style world models or policies.

Question: JEPA training is brittle because nothing principled stops representation collapse, so practitioners stack under-specified tricks and tune many hyperparameters. The paper asks two things. Which embedding distribution minimizes downstream risk when the downstream task is unknown? And can that distribution be enforced in a way that is provable, scales to high dimensions and large batches, and is distributed-friendly?

Method: On the theory side, the authors argue that anisotropic embeddings increase both the bias of ridge-regularized linear probes and the variance of unregularized OLS probes. For nonlinear probes (radius k-NN and Nadaraya–Watson kernel regression), the integrated squared bias scales with the Fisher information of the embedding density. Under a fixed scalar covariance constraint, the isotropic Gaussian uniquely minimizes that Fisher information. SIGReg then enforces this target in three steps:
- It projects the batch of embeddings onto M random unit directions, resampled every step and synced across GPUs.
- On each 1D projection, it runs the Epps–Pulley goodness-of-fit test, a weighted L2 distance between the empirical characteristic function and that of N(0,1), integrated with a 17-point trapezoid rule over [-5,5].
- It averages the per-direction statistics.

A Cramér–Wold argument justifies testing via 1D projections. Characteristic-function tests are preferred over two alternatives: moment-matching tests, which are non-identifiable with finitely many moments and have unbounded gradients, and CDF tests, which need sorting and are non-differentiable. The Epps–Pulley statistic has provably bounded gradients and curvature, runs in O(N) time and memory, and needs only an all_reduce under data-parallel training. The minibatch estimate carries an O(1/N) bias. The full loss is (1−λ) times a prediction term plus λ times SIGReg applied per view. The prediction term is the squared distance of every view's embedding to the mean of the global-view embeddings, DINO-style multi-crop with no predictor network. The core code is about 50 lines of PyTorch. With a mean/variance-only test, the objective reduces to VICReg, which the authors argue against.

Robots and setup: No robots, robot sensors, simulators or control tasks appear anywhere. The paper mentions action-conditioned robot data (DROID) only to motivate when a predictor network is justified, and never tests it. All experiments are image classification pretraining:
- Pretraining datasets: ImageNet-1K, ImageNet-100 and ImageNet-10, plus small in-domain sets (Galaxy10 with about 11k galaxy images, Flowers102 with about 1k, CIFAR-10/100, Food101).
- Transfer evaluation: DTD, Aircraft, Cars and Pets in addition to the above.
- Backbones: about 60 timm architectures, including ResNets, ViTs (up to ViT-H/14 and a 1.8B ViT-g), ConvNeXt-V2, Swin, MaxViT, LeViT and EfficientNet.
- Recipe: AdamW, 2 global 224px views plus 6 local 96px views, λ≈0.05.
- Evaluation: mostly frozen-backbone linear probes, with some full fine-tuning.
- Qualitative only: PCA feature maps and thresholded [CLS]-attention video object segmentation.

Results: On ImageNet-1K, frozen linear probing reaches 77.1% for ViT-L, 78.5% for ConvNeXtV2-H and 79% for ViT-H/14. There is no same-budget head-to-head against DINOv2-style training on ImageNet-1K.

In-domain Galaxy10 pretraining is the most striking result: small LeJEPA models beat transfer from frontier natural-image models.

| Galaxy10 setting | Best LeJEPA | DINOv3 ViT-S/16 | DINOv2 ViT-S |
|---|---|---|---|
| Frozen probe, all labels | 78.17 (ResNet-34) | 71.38 | 67.62 |
| Full fine-tuning, all labels | 83.28 (ResNet-34) | 81.60 | 78.34 |
| Full fine-tuning, 1-shot | 29.42 (ConvNeXt-V2 Nano) | 24.71 | — |

The flip side appears in Table 5: on natural-image datasets, an I-JEPA ViT-H pretrained on ImageNet-22k still clearly beats small in-domain LeJEPA models (e.g., CIFAR-100 86.9 vs about 70).

Transfer from ImageNet-1K (Table 2, averages over 8 datasets, all-shot):

| Model | Avg accuracy | Pretraining epochs |
|---|---|---|
| LeJEPA ViT-L | 79.48 | 100 |
| I-JEPA ViT-H | 78.50 | 300 |
| I-JEPA ViT-H + STOP | 80.70 | 300 |

LeJEPA beats plain I-JEPA with a smaller model and a third of the epochs, but I-JEPA+STOP wins on average at 1, 10 and all shots. The text's claim of "consistently outperform" is therefore overstated.

Across about 50 small timm models on ImageNet-10, all train without collapse and reach 91.5–95%. The training loss correlates with downstream linear-probe accuracy, with Spearman of roughly 85–99% depending on setting. Rescaling the loss by λ^0.4 pushes it to about 0.93–0.99. This enables label-free model selection, which is a practical plus.

Ablations: Performance is fairly flat over λ, with peaks around 0.01–0.05 that shift with the number of views. A single global view hurts badly (53% vs 72% at 4 views on ViT-L/IN-1K). On ViT-L/IN-1K:
- Batch size 128 works at 72.2%, versus 74.7% at 512.
- Shrinking the integration range to [-1,1] costs about 2 points.
- More slices help modestly; resampling directions each step matters far more than using many fixed ones.
- Register tokens make no difference.

Removing the predictor and teacher network does not cause collapse. Adding SWA or an EMA-teacher-like encoder gives small gains for ViTs, e.g., ViT-S 76.6→80.0 with a 1-layer projector. SIGReg costs under 1 ms per call for typical sizes on a V100.

Limitations: The optimality theory relies on strong assumptions, including an isotropic prior on target-function gradients, asymptotic small-bandwidth regimes and Sobolev smoothness of the embedding density. It addresses probe bias and variance rather than representation content. The empirical scope is image classification only. There are no video-prediction, action-conditioned, or robot experiments, and the 1.8B model is shown only through a training curve. There are some presentation sloppinesses, such as a Figure 17 caption with the colors swapped, and claims slightly ahead of the tables.

Takeaway: Read it if you pretrain your own visual encoders, especially on non-standard in-domain robot camera data where DINOv2/v3 transfer may underperform. Also read it if you want a collapse-proof, low-tuning JEPA regularizer to drop into a world-model pipeline. Algorithms 1–2 and Section 4 are the useful parts. Skip it if you are looking for robot learning results; there are none.

arxiv-2505-09603.text:
Gist: DataMIL adapts the datamodels framework from ML data attribution to robot imitation learning. It scores chunks of a large prior dataset by their estimated effect on a target task's performance, then co-trains a policy on the top-scoring chunks plus a few target demos. The pitch is that this "performance-aware" selection beats similarity heuristics, especially with heterogeneous data (OXE), unseen embodiments, and multi-task targets. It does so without running any policy rollouts during selection.

Question: Given a handful of task-specific demos and a big prior corpus, which prior data should you co-train on? Existing robotics methods retrieve data by similarity to the target demos: Behavior Retrieval (state-action VAE latents), FlowRetrieval (optical-flow VAE), STRAP (DinoV2 features plus dynamic time warping), or language. These proxies ignore whether a sample actually helps the policy. Datamodels address that in NLP and vision, but they normally require many train-and-evaluate cycles. In robotics, evaluation means real-world rollouts, so the open problem is making datamodels usable here.

Method: A linear datamodel assigns each prior cluster a score τ(z) for its additive effect on a target metric, and selection keeps the top x%. Two estimators are used:
1. A regression estimator: train many policies on random subsets and regress performance onto inclusion indicators. In MetaWorld this used m = 10^4 subsets with inclusion probability p = 0.1.
2. A metagradient estimator based on Metagradient Descent (Engstrom et al. 2025): differentiate exactly through the last k = 100 training steps with respect to per-sample weights, iterate T = 20 to 30 times, and average the gradients. This is used for the larger Octo policy.

The key robotics adaptation is the proxy metric. Instead of rollout success, it uses the negative behavior-cloning loss on held-out target demos, which needs no rollouts and is differentiable. The loss depends on the setting: L1 for the regression estimator, Gaussian NLL for the metagradient estimator in MetaWorld, and the diffusion denoising loss for Octo. In LIBERO, pre-grasp states are optionally upweighted 2x. Two further tricks reduce noise and shift:
- Prior data is clustered into sub-trajectories (length 15 in LIBERO) or whole trajectories (MetaWorld, OXE) to reduce estimate variance.
- For OXE, half of the target demos are mixed into datamodel training to reduce distribution shift, and the other half is used for the proxy.

The final policy is co-trained with a target sampling probability α = 0.5. MetaWorld is the exception: there it trains on selected data only, since co-training gave negligible gains.

Robots and setup: There are three settings.
- MetaWorld (simulated): all 50 tasks, using state-based goal-conditioned MLP Gaussian policies (a no-goal variant is in the appendix). The prior data is about 350K steps of scripted expert data plus 1M steps from a multi-task SAC replay buffer (21% average success), with 5 expert target demos per task.
- LIBERO (simulated): the 10 LIBERO-10 long-horizon tasks, with LIBERO-90 (4,500 teleoperated demos) as the prior and 5 target demos per task. The policy is Octo-small, a transformer diffusion policy on RGB images, with 10% of the prior selected.
- Real world: a Franka Panda and a PAL Tiago (an embodiment absent from the prior data). The prior data is subsets of 13, 23 or 24 OXE datasets from Octo's training mix, roughly 300k trajectories. There are four task settings: Franka-Ball (OXE-13, 10 demos, 1% selected), Franka-Pouch (OXE-23, 30 demos, 0.75%), Tiago-Sink (OXE-24, 20 demos, 0.5%), and Droid-Multitask (open drawer, bread in bowl, napkin in drawer; 40 demos, 1%). Target demos were collected with the TeleMoMa teleoperation system, and real-world policies are fine-tuned from Octo-small for 50k steps. The paper gives little sensor detail beyond RGB observations.

Results: Validating the proxy on MetaWorld pick-place-wall, top-10% selection reached roughly 88% success with true rollouts, about 86% with proxy plus regression, and about 81% with proxy plus metagradients. All-data reached about 13% and target-only about 2%; this pattern held on three more tasks. Averaged over 50 MetaWorld tasks, DataMIL is about 10 points above the best baseline (roughly 90% vs low 80s for BR/Flow) and also about 10 points better without goal conditioning.

On LIBERO-10 the gains are modest, with DataMIL averaging 37.76%:

| Method | LIBERO-10 avg. success |
|---|---|
| DataMIL | 37.76% |
| BR | 36.4% |
| Flow | 35.42% |
| STRAP | 34.96% |
| AR | 30.52% |
| All-Data | 27.72% |
| Target-only | 21.5% |

Per task, DataMIL is not uniformly best. STRAP wins Stove-Moka, Bowl-Cabinet, Book-Caddy and Mug-Pudding.

The real-robot results are the strongest claim, with DataMIL averaging 61.0%:

| Method | Real-robot avg. success |
|---|---|
| DataMIL | 61.0% |
| Flow | 40.0% |
| STRAP | 39.8% |
| BR | 39.4% |
| Random | 30.9% |
| AR | 24.1% |
| Target-only | 20.4% |

Per task:
- Franka-Pouch: 70.6% vs 41.2% for BR.
- Tiago-Sink: 64.1% vs 46.2%.
- Droid-Multitask: 59.4% vs 50.0% for Flow.
- Franka-Ball: STRAP's 57.1% beats DataMIL's 50.0%.

Qualitatively, DataMIL selects a broader mix of OXE sources, and its top five sources for Franka-Pouch are all Franka data. The baselines concentrate on single datasets, for example AR selects mostly RT-1 for Tiago and Flow selects mostly BC-Z for Franka-Pouch.

Ablations: All ablations are on LIBERO-5.
- Selection ratio: DataMIL's advantage is largest at 5 to 10% selection and disappears at 20% or more.
- Cluster size: length-15 sub-trajectories beat length 30 and whole trajectories.
- Co-training ratio: α = 0.5 was best.
- Longer training: training All-Data 2x or 4x longer did not help (43.36, 44.13, 38.40).
- STRAP setup: the authors note that their STRAP numbers are lower than the original paper's. They attribute this to final-checkpoint-only evaluation and using Octo instead of a Robomimic policy. They also modified STRAP to retrieve 10% of the data, which raised it from 24.72% to 34.96%.

Limitations and cost: Selection is expensive.
- Regression in MetaWorld took about 8 hours on 8×A100, amortized across the 50 tasks.
- The metagradient estimator runs 3 to 5x slower than normal training: 16 to 20 hours on 4 A5000s for LIBERO and 3 to 4 days on 4 A100s for OXE.

Hyperparameters such as selection ratio and cluster granularity lack principled defaults. The real-world evidence is thin: one seed and 14 to 39 trials per task, with partial credit given in Droid-Multitask. Targets are mostly single-task.

Takeaways: Read it if you curate co-training data from large heterogeneous corpora or care about cross-embodiment transfer. The main transferable insight is that held-out BC loss on a few target demos is a good enough, differentiable stand-in for rollout success to drive influence-based selection. The second is that this pays off most when similarity heuristics break down. Skim the LIBERO results, which are near-parity, and treat the large real-robot gaps as promising but statistically light.

arxiv-2611-05368.text:
Gist: GUILD is a closed-loop method for deciding which robot demonstrations to collect next. It is aimed at the case where the deployment environment is hard to access but auxiliary environments are not. A VLM proposes candidate data-collection tasks (scene, object configuration, goal). Then predictive data attribution (metagradients via MAGIC/REPLAY) estimates how much each task's trajectories help a small target-domain dataset, and the next teleoperation batch goes to the highest-utility task. It matters because it moves data curation from post-hoc filtering, where the cost of useless data has already been paid, to deciding upfront what to collect.

Question: Given an initial dataset, a learner, a target metric and a fixed collection budget, how should one choose a distribution over task parameters to collect so that training on the union maximizes deployment performance under distribution shift? Prior curation work (DataMIL, CUPID, STRAP, ReMix) assumes the data already exists. The closest guided-collection work, Factored Scaling Curves (FSC), needs predefined factors and trains many policies per factor. GUILD targets open-ended task spaces using only one attribution computation per iteration.

Method: There are two timescales. In the outer loop, a VLM (GPT-5.2) receives target-task video frames, a language description and the available assets, and proposes m candidate tasks. A uniform seed of demos is collected for each. At scheduled points (LIBERO after iterations 2, 4, 8, 16; real world after 3 and 9), the VLM proposes new tasks conditioned on a utility-ranked list of previous tasks. An explore/exploit split mixes ranking-conditioned and context-only proposals.

In the inner loop, the policy's data weights are treated as meta-parameters, and the gradient of an offline proxy metric (validation loss on the target demos) with respect to per-trajectory weights is computed exactly via REPLAY metagradients. Trajectory scores are averaged per task to give a marginal utility U(φ). The argmax task then receives the next batch of b demos (hard selection), and utilities are recomputed. A softmax "soft-sampling" variant is also studied.

Robots and setup: The simulation uses LIBERO-90, holding out one of 17 scenes per target and collecting from the other 16 with scripted pick-and-place policies. Tasks are parameterized as (scene, pick object, place region). The three targets are book-caddy, soup-butter-tray and bowl-ketchup-drawer (also called ketchup-bowl-cabinet in places). The real-world setup has six environments: two kitchens, two bathrooms and two offices, built with tablecloths, appliances and green-screen backgrounds. Demonstrations are collected by human teleoperation with TeleMoMa, with 1–3 distractors per trajectory. The paper does not name the exact robot model or camera/sensor configuration. The four real targets are pink-cup-sink, towel-drawer-close, bowl-pour and lemon-drawer-close, using 15–50 target demos. Two real settings are evaluated:
- Closed-World: selection from a pre-collected pool of 49 tasks.
- Open-World: the VLM writes free-form scene configurations and instructions, given 11 movable objects.

The policy is language-conditioned Octo-Small fine-tuned from the released checkpoint, co-trained 50/50 with the target data (10k steps in sim, 25k in real). Baselines are Random, VLM-Uniform, STRAP (DINOv2 + DTW similarity), FSC (Group-t, offline embedding-similarity variant), All-Data and Target-Only.

Results: On LIBERO (3 collection seeds × 5 policy seeds × 100 rollouts), GUILD matches or beats the best baseline at all budgets. Final success is 68.2 / 69.6 / 56.9% (average 64.9%). Read from the plots, FSC averages about 61%, VLM-Uniform and STRAP about 54–55%, and Random about 36%.

In real Closed-World (20 rollouts per policy), GUILD averages roughly 58% versus about 38% for FSC and VLM-Uniform, and also beats All-Data. All-Data includes target-environment data and reaches roughly 42%. In Open-World, only GUILD and VLM-Uniform were run; GUILD reaches roughly 72% versus 47%, the "~25%" average gain the authors cite. Both methods do better in Open-World than in Closed-World.

Against humans, about six LIBERO participants are plotted, although the text says 8 roboticists were surveyed. They average roughly 55%, about the same as VLM-Uniform and below GUILD's ~65%, with some individuals beating GUILD on single tasks. Two real-world experts with 4–5 years of experience score roughly 50–55% average in Open-World, and their results are inconsistent across tasks.

Ablations: Removing ranking feedback from support expansion drops the LIBERO average to 59.2%, mostly on soup-butter-tray (55.3 vs 69.6). Soft-sampling gives 61.3%. Swapping in Gemini-2.5-Flash gives 61.1% on average, with large per-task swings (−17 points on soup-butter-tray, +7 on bowl-ketchup-drawer). Explore-exploit beats pure exploitation on bowl-ketchup-drawer (56.9 vs 50.7%). Dataset-level utility correlates with downstream success on two tasks (Spearman 0.78 and 0.75) but weakly negatively on book-caddy (−0.23). Many high-allocation tasks were introduced in later expansion rounds, and the final allocations range from concentrated to diffuse depending on the target.

Limitations and caveats: Each attribution step takes 10–15 minutes on four A5000 GPUs. A full run takes 7–8 hours for LIBERO and 10–15 hours in the real world, and smaller batches trade compute for adaptivity. The VLM can propose infeasible or unoriginal tasks. The task space is discretized by the VLM rather than treated as continuous. Several limitations are not emphasized by the authors:
- Real-world evaluation is 20 rollouts per policy, and Open-World comparisons are limited to two methods plus two experts.
- The validation-loss proxy is only loosely validated against success.
- The human study sizes are small.
- Some task names are inconsistent across the paper.

Takeaway: Read it if you work on data collection, curation or co-training for imitation learning. Its main contribution is a practical recipe that uses exact metagradient attribution as an online acquisition signal on top of VLM task proposals. The evidence is consistent but modest in scale, and its most interesting claim is beating experienced roboticists' intuition.

arxiv-2611-06881.text:
Gist: The paper introduces VABAR, a simulation benchmark of six industrial, medical and infrastructure manipulation tasks. It targets "agentic robotics" systems, in which LLM coding agents compose and parameterize skill programs, rather than end-to-end visuomotor policies. It frames these tasks as "Variational Automation": a fixed operational objective that must hold across a structured, bounded distribution of object, pose and layout variations. The benchmark comes with assets, a skill library, human-authored reference solutions and initial baselines. It is mainly worth reading if you build LLM-driven program-synthesis or skill-composition systems for manipulation and want a harder, application-flavored testbed than household pick-and-place suites.

Question: Existing benchmarks such as LIBERO, ManiSkill and SimplerEnv focus on household pick-and-place, evaluate language-conditioned learned policies, and are increasingly saturated. They also tend to treat variation as a perturbation around a nominal task rather than as the intended operating range. The authors ask how to fairly evaluate agentic systems that differ widely in internal representations, tools and controllers. Their answer is to measure only externally observable task success under controlled variation tiers. They also ask how success, cycle time and failure modes change as variation increases.

Method: A VA task class is formalized as a tuple of environment frames, robot spec, admissible assets, admissible configuration space, a sampling distribution over configurations, and a success condition. Variations are constrained to preserve:
- the identity of the task,
- physical and robot-reachability feasibility,
- a graded difficulty,
- solvability with the same skill set.

The authors list seven benchmark design criteria: agentic relevance, application relevance, accessibility, controlled diversity, repeatability via seeds, computational efficiency, and versioned durability. They also define a diagnostic execution record that separates errors into four stages:
- perception (observation to estimated state),
- decision (estimated state to action),
- physical interaction (action to next state and contacts),
- verification.

This record uses privileged simulator state and contact logs. Success conditions are written in an extended BDDL covering both rigid and deformable objects. The authors also extend their Modular Open Robot Skill Library (MORSL) to 33 skills, 25 of them new, covering:
- functional-feature localization,
- source-destination correspondence,
- in-hand registration,
- staged feature mating,
- cable centerline tracking, anchoring and routing,
- verification checks.

Robots and setup: The single-arm Franka (model not further specified) is used for the rigid tasks, including gear meshing. A bimanual YAM platform is used for cable insertion and cable routing. The six tasks are:
- tool sorting into labeled bins,
- tool hanging on a pegboard,
- gear meshing onto axles followed by a button press,
- syringe packing into a disposal box with distractors,
- USB-C cable insertion,
- cable routing around an ordered peg sequence.

Each task has two difficulty levels, for example singulated versus cluttered objects, two versus three gears, or 2–3 versus 4–6 pegs. The asset library has over 55 assets. Two implementations exist: one on the NVIDIA Newton physics engine (rigid plus deformable multiphysics) and one on Isaac Lab Arena, run on NVIDIA L40 GPU nodes; the two differ in textures, lighting, assets and robot setup. Perception uses SAM3-based segmentation. Camera and sensor configurations are not described in detail, and there is no real-robot component or dataset of demonstrations. Each task-difficulty condition uses 30 generated instances. The Isaac Lab Arena numbers fall on multiples of 2.5%, which hints at a different trial count. Tool sorting and hanging are scored per object; sequential tasks such as gear meshing are scored per episode.

Results: Four systems are compared:
- a human-authored GaP computation graph over MORSL skills, run on Newton and on Isaac Lab Arena,
- Claude Code with Claude Opus 5 and no robotics harness or skills,
- GaP with the graph generated autonomously by the same model.

The human graphs on Newton set the reference, for example:

| Task | Level 1 success | Level 2 success |
|---|---|---|
| Tool sorting | 47.1% | 33.7% |
| Tool hanging | 86.7% | 81.7% |
| Gear meshing | 100% | 90% |
| Syringe packing | 87% | 63% |
| Cable insertion | 86.7% | 30% |
| Cable routing | 46.7% | 46.7% |

Bare Claude Code is near zero everywhere. Its only nonzero results are 16.7% and 10% on tool hanging and 3.3% on Level 1 cable routing. Autonomous GaP lands in between:

| Task | Level 1 success | Level 2 success |
|---|---|---|
| Tool sorting | 26.7% | 13.3% |
| Tool hanging | 33.3% | 10% |
| Gear meshing | 70% | 60% |
| Syringe packing | 33.3% | 12.1% |
| Cable insertion | 36.7% | 23.3% |
| Cable routing | 36.7% | 13.3% |

GaP beats Claude Code in 11 of 12 conditions and ties at 10% on Level 2 tool hanging, but trails the human graphs in every condition. The human graph transferred to Isaac Lab Arena generally degrades. Examples are syringe packing Level 1 (52.5% at a 939 s median cycle time) and cable routing Level 2 (5%). The Level 2 tool sorting cell is missing. Cycle times are medians over successful trials only, so they are confounded by which instances succeed. For example, autonomous GaP shows a shorter tool-sorting cycle (134 s) than the human graph (422 s). In the failure breakdown, motion and insertion errors dominate in many settings, reaching 96% on Level 2 cable insertion. Perception failures rise in clutter, for example 56% on Level 2 tool sorting and 58% on Level 2 syringe packing. A Newton ground-truth inspection of jammed syringes is shown as a qualitative diagnosis example.

Limitations: The evaluation is preliminary.
- There are only two difficulty tiers and one LLM.
- There are no learned-policy, VLA or non-GaP agentic baselines, despite the stated aim of comparing architectures.
- There is no ablation separating harness from skill library, which the authors acknowledge.
- There is no sim-to-real validation, despite "physical realizability" and "predictive of real-world success" being listed as criteria.
- The GaP harness and MORSL come from the same group, so the main agentic baseline is the authors' own system.

Some narrative claims do not match the tables. The text says perception and grasping are highly reliable in low-variation settings, yet grasp failures are 51% on Level 1 tool sorting and 45% on Level 1 cable routing. It says tool-hanging success is stable across tiers, which holds for the human graph but not for autonomous GaP (33% to 10%). The failure table reports N/A for Level 1 gear meshing, which is consistent with the human graph's 100% but not with autonomous GaP's 70%. This leaves unclear which system the failure analysis covers and how failures were attributed.

Takeaway: The useful contributions are the VA framing, the task and variation specifications, the extended skill library, and the observation that even human-authored graphs reach only about 30–47% on the harder insertion, routing and sorting conditions. That suggests real headroom rather than saturation. The empirical section is thin and best read as a baseline sketch. Skim Sections III–V and Tables I–III unless you plan to use the benchmark or the MORSL/GaP stack directly.

pdf-beb8536dd7.text:
Gist: This is not a research paper. It is an FDA (CDRH) discussion paper and request for feedback, dated November 2026, on how to weigh benefits and risks of robotic medical devices that have autonomous and/or remote teleoperation capabilities. It proposes shared terminology, lists candidate benefits, risks, and mitigations, and poses 15 open questions ahead of a public workshop on December 2–3, 2026. It matters because it signals how the US regulator is framing surgical and medical robot autonomy and telesurgery before any such systems are authorized. The paper notes that, as of July 2026, no remotely teleoperated or fully autonomous robotic device system has US marketing authorization. It explicitly states that it is not draft or final guidance and does not set policy.

Question: The paper asks how FDA should characterize and weigh benefits and risks for robotic systems as control shifts from the user to the machine (autonomy), or as the user moves out of the room (remote teleoperation). It also asks what evidence and risk controls could provide "reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness" for these systems. The gap it identifies is the lack of agreed terminology and evaluation expectations. Scope extends beyond robotically-assisted surgical devices (RASDs) to stereotactic navigation, robotic imaging, and endoluminal navigation systems.

Method: The approach is conceptual, not experimental. Key definitions:
- Autonomy is the ability to perform tasks and make decisions from current state and sensing without user intervention.
- Autonomy is explicitly distinguished from "automaticity," meaning predictable rule-following behavior. The paper focuses only on autonomy in this stronger sense.
- Remote teleoperation is real-time control by a user not physically in the room with the patient. It can range from single tasks to entire procedures, and from another room in the same facility to another country. Connections may be wired (fiber) or wireless (Wi-Fi, 5G, satellite).

The paper reviews autonomy frameworks. Yang et al. (2017) is described as the most widely adopted; it has six procedure-level levels, from Level 0 (full surgeon control) to Level 5 (full autonomy). More granular alternatives are IEC/TR 60601-4-1 Degree of Autonomy, Haidegger's Level of Autonomy, and Schmidgall et al. (2025). These decompose autonomy into four cognitive functions: monitor, generate, select, and execute. The paper notes this granularity costs practicality as a grouping tool. It then maps benefits, risks, and mitigations onto existing FDA benefit-risk guidance factors.

Robots and setup: There are no robots, sensors, simulators, datasets, or experiments. No specific robot models are named. The paper cites only motivating examples:
- remote robotic ultrasound
- remote RASD teleoperation
- an FDA-authorized autonomous peripheral blood-draw robot
- DARPA's MEDICS program for autonomous hemorrhage control
- a 2025 Johns Hopkins report of a realistic autonomous surgery
- the 2001 transatlantic telesurgery (Marescaux et al.)
- a 2025 industry consensus paper on network and facility requirements for remote robotic surgery

Results: There are no quantitative results or baselines. The substantive output is a qualitative catalogue.

Claimed autonomy benefits include consistency and repeatability, fewer errors from inexperience, better use of pre-procedure imaging, broader access, and reduced user burden. AI/ML could amplify these benefits through adaptive planning.

Autonomy risks include:
- errors executed before a supervisor can intervene
- poor adaptation to unanticipated conditions such as tissue deformation, bleeding, or anomalous anatomy
- slow control handover
- automation bias and automation rejection
- deskilling, where users cannot finish a procedure manually if the system fails
- AI/ML failures out of the training distribution, subgroup performance disparities, opacity, and performance drift
- cybersecurity exposure under FD&C Act Section 524B

Teleoperation benefits center on time-critical care such as stroke thrombectomy and MI, specialist access, and remote proctoring. Teleoperation risks include:
- delayed management of intraprocedural adverse events
- connectivity loss
- motion-control and audio-visual delays that are out of sync with each other
- missing sensory cues, such as drill pitch, palpation resistance, and odors
- difficulty converting to a manual procedure or transferring the patient

The paper also notes two tensions. Staffing both a remote and a local specialist may reduce overall specialist availability. And the locations with the most to gain from teleoperation are often the riskiest because they lack on-site resources.

Combined autonomy-and-teleoperation risks: Combining the two capabilities raises latency during autonomous failure and unreliable handoffs between autonomous and teleoperated modes. Shared risks across both include dependence on sensors and imaging, hardware and software failures, team training gaps, and end-to-end cybersecurity. The cybersecurity concerns are network performance, system-level threats, command integrity and non-repudiation, availability, and users' inability to detect tampered video.

Mitigations considered: The paper discusses design controls (haptic boundaries, velocity and force limits, redundancy and fail-safes). It covers verification and validation through bench, in silico, cadaver, and clinical studies under worst-case conditions. It also covers training the in-room staff for override and emergency stop, human factors engineering, and postmarket monitoring through real-world data and Medical Device Reporting. It suggests benefit-risk may need to be procedure- or condition-specific. For example, remote coronary stent deployment is likely riskier than advancing a GI endoscope.

Limitations: The document is high-level and non-binding. It offers no thresholds for latency, accuracy, or autonomy level, no proposed test protocols, and no data. It deliberately avoids saying what evidence FDA would actually require.

Takeaway: Read it if you work on surgical or medical autonomy, shared control, or telesurgery and care about clinical translation. It is a compact map of the failure modes and evidence types the regulator is worried about, and the 15 questions are a good source of research problems. Examples include override latency, safe mode handoff, sensory substitution, worst-case validation, and robustness to connectivity degradation. Skip it if you want technical methods or empirical results; it contains none.
